title: The Fractured Isles
signs_note: Deliberately none. The Isles used to carry six painted area names - THE CRUMBLING COAST, FIGHT FOR THE LEDGE, THE FIRST CROSSING, THE LONG BRIDGE, THE DEEP ISLES, THE ARCHWAY - and they are gone. Signs are for introducing things, and by the time anyone reaches this level they have played First Steps, which is where the coast, the bandits and the rocks get introduced. Naming a stretch here is captioning a picture the player can already read. First Steps keeps three, for the three things it is the first to show.
scope: Level 1. Area 1 The Crumbling Coast and Area 2 The Bridge Ambush, as one continuous course. Area 3 The Archway is the boss platform, and the boss is the dragon.
brief: Cross the breaking coast, hold the bridge, climb the broken isles.
note: Opening rebuilt to the Magic Cliffs demo scene: mesa (tree at the left) -> bridge -> mesa -> a jumped chasm -> the pierced archway rock, which meets the original course at x1452. The hanging stalactite and the archway mass are rock_mass set dressing (features/world/scenery.gd), not collision. Flat grass line y648. Everything from x1452 on is the original course.
solids_note: The two island_large at 7116 and 7548 belong to the boss platform, and they are the only reason the dragon can be fought rather than waited out: it cruises 156 above the deck and a jump from the floor reaches 143. 96 up against a 107 apex, the same as The Dragon's Roost. The optional fifth value names the art the rectangle wears. Without one it is a grassed cliff; with one it is that piece, centred and sitting on the top edge. Collision is the rectangle either way.
hazards_note: Deliberately none. The Fractured Isles kills by the fall, not by spikes: every threat here is a gap you misjudged or a bandit who reached you. Spikes are instant death regardless of health, which would undercut the health-bar fight the level is built around.
decor_note: [x, y, piece] with the piece's bottom edge at y and x its centre. Plants stand on a surface; vine and vine_rock hang DOWN a cliff face, so their y is below the lip and their own dark backing is kept because it matches the rock. Art only, never collision. scripts/check_levels.py warns if a standing plant is left hanging.
enemies_note:
Two on the deck and one waiting on the far side, so the crossing is fought from both directions. A blast staggers whichever is closer. The one on the Archway platform is the dragon, and it is a flyer: it sits on the deck until the story card at 6960 wakes it - see cutscene_note, and its own 560 of aggro is the fallback if anything ever removes that - then it alternates between fighting from the air and landing to fight on its feet. Every altitude it holds is measured from the height it took off at, which is why the Archway deck is flat at 660 across its whole width and has to stay that way. A fourth value "perch" marks an enemy that does NOT hold its section's gate: the six on the high ledges cannot be reached on foot and the blast flies flat, so a gate that waited for them could never open. They are harassment, not a lock.

THE DRAGON WAS TOO EASY and is not any more. 1500 health is twenty-five clean hits of the hardest blow the player owns; it was 240, which is four. With that came the rest of being a boss: it hits through the player's blows and is never staggered or turned out of a swing (`unflinching`), every blow it lands throws him off his feet and the breath throws hardest, it swoops pass after pass instead of circling (`swoop_cooldown` 0.55, was 1.4), it decides to breathe from 440 rather than from inside the flame's own 121..240 band - which is why the breath used to be thrown exactly zero times in thirty seconds - and a spammed blast stacks against the player rather than holding it off for ever. scripts are no help here: tests/diag_dragonfight.gd is the measurement and the place to re-take it.
boss_arena_note:
The x the dragon fight is sealed behind, and the west edge of the room both of them are shut into - the player by a wall built in _build_arena (game/session.gd), the dragon by fly_bounds. 6912 is the lip of the deck it stands on. Its SECTION opens at 6110, which is out in the middle of the chasm: sealing there would leave the four stepping stones inside the fight - the ledges he crossed to get here - and stand the wall in mid-air over the water, where hitting it means falling. 6912 is ground. The camera stops against it the same way it stops against a gate, 48 px inside the screen, so you can see you have run out of screen rather than out of floor.

It shuts once he is a wall's width past the line and the boss is awake, and opens the moment the body is gone. The flag at 7932 is past the gate at 7800 and therefore outside the arena, so nothing about this can shut him in with the level finished. Measured by tests/diag_arena_seal.gd: holding left for twelve seconds and a running jump west both stop at 6920, and the dragon gets no further west than 6912 either.
gates_note:
The x of each section's end wall. Four gates make five sections, and the fifth has none: it is the 132 px of deck between the Archway wall and the flag, and there is nothing left in it. A gate is shut while any enemy in its section still holds it, and while it is shut the camera stops with it at the right edge of the screen and an invisible wall stands on the line - you have run out of screen, not out of floor. Clearing the section opens both. Walking back is never blocked. Positions are chokepoints read off the level's own geometry: 2240 is the lip before the first crossing, 4460 the end of the long bridge's floor, 6110 the last of the deep isles before the hops to the Archway, and 7800 the far end of the Archway itself.

That last one closes a real hole rather than framing a fight. The Dragon Lord used to stand on the ground between you and the flag; the dragon that replaced him cruises 156 overhead and blocks nothing, so the boss could be run straight past and the level finished without a blow struck. The dragon perches at 7650, inside the section, so it holds the wall until it is beaten. The arena that leaves is the 888 px from the mouth of the Archway at 6912 to the wall, which is what the two floating stones are spaced across, and the camera stops at 7368 with the wall on the right edge.

The wall is the dragon's limit too, not just the player's. session.gd fences a flyer into the section it was placed in - see fly_bounds in features/combat/enemy.gd - because a flyer has no floor to run out from under it and backs away from a player who crowds it, so one cornered against a shut gate would otherwise be pushed out through the side of the screen. tests/diag_arena.gd is the measurement: 272 frames of 900 off screen before the fence, none after.

The wall at 7800 also stays shut through the dragon's whole death, not just until its health runs out: a beaten boss holds its section until its BODY is gone - see section_clear in game/session.gd. The flag is 132 px past the wall and the death takes seconds, so without that a player who beat the dragon backed against the wall reached the flag in 0.82 s against the 2.05 s the departure card needs, and finished the level without ever seeing the ending. tests/diag_endcard.gd measures it.
music_note:
A file in godot/audio/ without its extension, played for as long as the level is. Omit it and the level is silent - both greybox slices are. The Fractured Isles and the title screen name the same loop, which is the one the Magic Cliffs pack ships, so starting a new journey carries straight on from the menu rather than restarting the track.

`boss_music` is the loop that takes over for as long as the dragon is fighting - xDeviruchi's Decisive Battle, copied in by scripts/extract_boss_music.py. session.gd asks current_track() every tick rather than cueing it at the moment the fight starts, because that is not the only way in and out of one: dying puts the player back at the spawn with the boss on its perch, and the level's own loop has to come back with him. It ends with the killing blow. The two seconds the dragon lies there, the departure card and the fly-away are the aftermath, and the level's own loop is the bed for all three - a battle track under the picture of it leaving would undo the picture. The boss PLATE outlasts the track on purpose: an empty bar under a departing dragon is the point of it.

cutscene.caption: Wow! A drake! What's it doing here??

cutscene_note:
The two story panels the dragon fight is bracketed by, and what brings each one up. `panel` names a file in ui/art/storyboard and `audio`/`out_audio` name files in audio/, both without their extensions, all written by scripts/extract_storyboard.py. `caption` is the line printed under the picture, in the same column and on the same scrim the opening's subtitles use - one line held for the whole card, because a card is one beat and not a scene with a script. The Dragon's Roost carries them on both of its start panels.

THE STANDOFF plays as he steps onto the Archway. `at` is the x he has to cross ON HIS FEET - the line is on the mouth of an arena you jump into, and without the footing test the picture could come up over a player frozen in mid-air who then drops out of the bottom of it. 6960 is 48 px past the mouth at 6912 and 690 short of the dragon, which is outside its 560 of aggro on purpose: the picture is what starts the fight, not the walk into it. session.gd stops the level where it stands, holds the card for as long as its clip runs, and on the way out wakes the boss and plays the roar over the dissolve - so what the picture dissolves into is the dragon already getting up and coming.

THE DEPARTURE plays when the dragon has finished FALLING. `after: "boss_down"` waits out the whole down beat - the 0.86 s collapse the pack draws and then DOWN_TIME lying on the deck, two seconds all told - and not for the body to leave, because the picture is of the dragon in the air on its way out and it belongs between the fall and the leaving. The card stops the world with the body still down, and the dragon gets up and climbs out of the level the moment the picture is gone.

BOTH CAN BE SKIPPED - both carry `"skip": true`, as every card in the game now does. They were unskippable, and the argument was that they are four and ten seconds, they play once per visit, and between them they are the only story this level tells, so a player who taps space out of habit at the first frame would never see either. What that argument misses is the second visit: someone on their fifth attempt at the dragon has already seen both, and holding them there is not storytelling. The first-frame-habit problem is real and is handled by the cards being once per visit rather than by refusing the key.

The keys are still SWALLOWED while a card is up, which is a separate guarantee and the one that matters: escape reaches the card and goes no further, so it cannot pause the game behind the picture and strand it there. Once per visit and not again on a retry: a cutscene standing between a player and another go at the boss is the one everybody learns to hate.
